Synthetic orders

Source: vignettes/articles/guide-synthetic-orders.Rmd
guide-synthetic-orders.Rmd

A synthetic order is an order that no Indian exchange offers, such as a bracket, a trailing stop, an iceberg or an order sliced over half an hour. UBI’s order engine builds each one out of ordinary broker orders: it places them, watches them, changes them and cancels them for you. The R/orders_*.R files of tradeR hold one R6 class for each of the fifty-four types the engine runs. Each class only describes the order and sends the description; all the work happens in UBI.

These are real orders.

place() sends real orders through UBI to real brokers, with real money. Many of these types keep acting after place() has returned: a trigger fires hours later, a trailing stop moves all day, a grid trades back and forth, a good-till-triggered order waits for up to a year. Construct every order with dry_run = TRUE first, which has UBI build the first broker request and return it without recording or sending anything.

UBI’s order engine must be running.

UBI’s order engine runs every synthetic order, and it places every other order too. While it is stopped, UBI refuses the order with HTTP 503 and nothing is queued. Order engine explains what it does.

The table below lists the three classes every synthetic order is built from, and the members they all share.

Kind Member Description
class SyntheticOrder The shared base: an order template plus the synthetic type that works it.
places orders place Sends the order to UBI’s order engine through place_order.
field parent_id UBI’s id for the order once place() has sent it, or NULL before that and after a dry run.
places orders cancel Cancels the order, with every leg it still has resting at a broker.
active binding parent The order as UBI’s order engine holds it now.
active binding orders, trades Today’s broker orders the order placed, and their trades.
class OrderCandidate One leg of an order that spans several instruments.
class ExposureWatch One watched instrument of an exposure hedge.
class PlanOrder An order described as a tree of parts, which can combine the other types in one order.

All fifty-four types

The table below lists every class, in its family. The file and class names spell out UBI’s abbreviations, so UBI’s oto is one_triggers_other here and its atr_trail is average_true_range_trail. The settings are the class’s own arguments, named as UBI names them except for average_true_range_multiple, which UBI calls atr_multiple, and for arguments that take an instrument object where UBI takes an id. Every class also takes reduce_only and hold_limits, described under Reduce-only orders and Holding limit orders. The last column is UBI’s first answer: 200 means a broker order goes out when you ask, and 202 means the engine records the order and waits for a price or a time. A type marked “or 202 when held” holds its limit orders by default and so answers 202.

Class File UBI type Family What it does Key settings First answer
SimpleOrder R/orders_simple.R simple Plain and laddered One plain order to one broker, with nothing watching it afterwards. Asking for it by name is useful only to set closes_position. none 200
FreezeSlicerOrder R/orders_freeze_slicer.R freeze_slicer Plain and laddered Splits an order above the exchange’s freeze quantity into even orders that each fit, all at one broker. none 200, or 202 when held
LadderOrder R/orders_ladder.R ladder Plain and laddered Places several limit orders spaced evenly between two prices, sharing the quantity between them. from_price, to_price, steps 200, or 202 when held
GridOrder R/orders_grid.R grid Plain and laddered Rests buys below the market and sells above it, and each fill places its opposite one step away. levels, step_points, most_inventory 200
ScaleWithProfitTakerOrder R/orders_scale_with_profit_taker.R scale_with_profit_taker Plain and laddered A ladder whose every filled rung gets its own profit-taker, and is placed again once that profit is taken. from_price, to_price, steps, profit_points, most_cycles 200, or 202 when held
TwoSidedQuoteOrder R/orders_two_sided_quote.R two_sided_quote Plain and laddered A bid and an offer kept around the fair price, leaning away from the inventory they build. half_spread_points, most_inventory, skew_ticks, step_ticks, fair_price 200
OneTriggersOtherOrder R/orders_one_triggers_other.R oto Linked orders Places a second order, sized to what actually filled, once the first one fills. then_transaction_type, then_order_type, then_price, then_trigger_price, then_product, then_validity 200, or 202 when held
OneCancelsOtherOrder R/orders_one_cancels_other.R oco Linked orders Rests a stop and a target on a position already held, each shrinking as the other fills. stop_price, stop_limit_price, target_price 200
BracketOrder R/orders_bracket.R bracket Linked orders An entry that arms a stop and a target behind itself on its first fill, even a partial one. stop_price, stop_limit_price, target_price 200, or 202 when held
CoverOrder R/orders_cover.R cover Linked orders An entry with a compulsory stop and no target. stop_price, stop_limit_price 200, or 202 when held
ScaleOutOrder R/orders_scale_out.R scale_out Linked orders A bracket with several targets that take the position off in tranches, and a stop that moves to breakeven. target_prices, stop_price, stop_limit_price, breakeven_after 200, or 202 when held
TwoSidedBreakoutOrder R/orders_two_sided_breakout.R two_sided_breakout Linked orders A buy stop above a range and a sell stop below it, where the first to fire cancels the other, with exits set a distance from the fill. buy_trigger, buy_limit, sell_trigger, sell_limit, and stop_distance with stop_limit_offset, target_distance or both 200
OneCancelsAllOrder R/orders_one_cancels_all.R oca Linked orders Several candidate entries, each on its own instrument, where the first fill cancels all the rest. candidates 200, or 202 when held
AttachedHedgeOrder R/orders_attached_hedge.R attached_hedge Linked orders Hedges each fill of the entry in another instrument, by a ratio or by an option’s delta, in whole lots. hedge_instrument, ratio or delta_volatility 200
MarketIfTouchedOrder R/orders_market_if_touched.R market_if_touched Price triggers Waits unseen for the price to touch a level, then takes what is there with a marketable limit. trigger_price, trigger_direction, buffer_ticks, trigger_on, hold_seconds 202
LimitIfTouchedOrder R/orders_limit_if_touched.R limit_if_touched Price triggers Waits for the price to touch a level, then rests a limit at another price. trigger_price, limit_price, trigger_direction, trigger_on, hold_seconds 202
CrossInstrumentOrder R/orders_cross_instrument.R cross_instrument Price triggers A limit-if-touched order whose trigger watches the last price of a different instrument. watch_instrument, trigger_price, limit_price, trigger_direction, trigger_on, hold_seconds 202
IndicatorTriggeredOrder R/orders_indicator_triggered.R indicator_triggered Price triggers Sends a limit when one field of the live quote, such as the day’s average price, crosses a level. trigger_price, limit_price, watch_field, trigger_direction 202
GoodTillTriggeredOrder R/orders_good_till_triggered.R gtt Price triggers A limit-if-touched order that keeps waiting across days until it fires or expires. trigger_price, limit_price, valid_days, trigger_direction, trigger_on, hold_seconds 202
CloseOnTriggerOrder R/orders_close_on_trigger.R close_on_trigger Price triggers At a level, cancels every order on the instrument to free margin, then closes the whole position. trigger_price, trigger_direction, trigger_on, hold_seconds 202
StopAndReverseOrder R/orders_stop_and_reverse.R stop_and_reverse Price triggers At a level, closes the position and opens the same size the other way. trigger_price, method, trigger_direction, trigger_on, hold_seconds 202
AccountConditionalOrder R/orders_account_conditional.R account_conditional Price triggers Sends an order when free margin, the day’s profit or the open position count reaches a level, or cancels it then. account_field, account_level, trigger_direction, action 202, or 200 with action = "cancel"
HiddenStopOrder R/orders_hidden_stop.R hidden_stop Stops and trailing A stop kept inside UBI that watches the bid or the offer, with an optional real stop behind it. trigger_price, backstop_price, backstop_limit_price, buffer_ticks, trigger_direction 202, or 200 with a backstop
CandleCloseStopOrder R/orders_candle_close_stop.R candle_close_stop Stops and trailing A hidden stop that fires only when a whole bar closes past the level. trigger_price, bar_minutes, backstop_price, backstop_limit_price, buffer_ticks, trigger_direction 202, or 200 with a backstop
TrailingStopOrder R/orders_trailing_stop.R trailing_stop Stops and trailing A real stop at the broker whose trigger follows the market up, never down. stop_limit_offset, trail_points or trail_percent, step_ticks, activate_at 200, or 202 with activate_at
TrailingEntryOrder R/orders_trailing_entry.R trailing_entry Stops and trailing A stop entry that follows a falling market down, so the first bounce of the trailing distance fills it. stop_limit_offset, trail_points or trail_percent, step_ticks, activate_at 200, or 202 with activate_at
AverageTrueRangeTrailOrder R/orders_average_true_range_trail.R atr_trail Stops and trailing A trailing stop whose distance is a multiple of the recent average true range. trail_points, stop_limit_offset, bar_minutes, periods, average_true_range_multiple, step_ticks, activate_at 200, or 202 with activate_at
DailyStopOrder R/orders_daily_stop.R daily_stop Stops and trailing A native stop placed afresh every trading morning for a position held overnight. stop_price, stop_limit_price, arm_at, valid_days 202
SteppedStopOrder R/orders_stepped_stop.R stepped_stop Stops and trailing A native stop moved to set levels at set profits, and switched to trailing at the last. entry_price, stop_price, stop_limit_offset, rules, step_ticks 200
PegOrder R/orders_peg.R peg Book-following limits A limit order kept re-priced to your own side’s best price, the midpoint or the other side as the book moves. reference, offset_ticks, cap_price 200
ChaserOrder R/orders_chaser.R chaser Book-following limits A limit order that starts on its own side of the book and steps towards the other until it fills. step_ticks, step_seconds, cap_price, cross_after_seconds 200
PostOnlyOrder R/orders_post_only.R post_only Book-following limits A limit order checked to rest rather than trade before it is sent. on_crossing 200
DiscretionaryOrder R/orders_discretionary.R discretionary Book-following limits A limit order that shows one price and quietly takes a slightly worse one when it comes within reach. discretion_points, discretion_quantity 200
VirtualLimitOrder R/orders_virtual_limit.R virtual_limit Book-following limits A limit order held inside UBI and sent only when the other side of the book reaches its price. Every plain day limit order now runs as this type. paper 202
MarketableLimitOrder R/orders_marketable_limit.R marketable_limit Book-following limits A market order sent as a limit a few ticks past the other side’s best price, which follows that price until it fills and is cancelled after a time. Every plain market order now runs as this type. buffer_ticks, fill_within_seconds 200, or 409 on an empty book
UnderlyingPegOrder R/orders_underlying_peg.R underlying_peg Book-following limits Moves a resting limit by delta times another instrument’s move, such as an option bid following the index. watch_instrument, delta, lowest_price, highest_price, step_ticks 200
VolatilityOrder R/orders_volatility.R volatility Book-following limits Prices an option from an implied volatility with Black-76, and re-prices it as the underlying and time move. watch_instrument, volatility, interest_rate, lowest_price, highest_price, step_ticks 200
TimeWeightedAveragePriceOrder R/orders_time_weighted_average_price.R twap Execution algorithms A large order sent as equal slices at even intervals over a period. slices, over_minutes 200, or 202 when held
VolumeWeightedAveragePriceOrder R/orders_volume_weighted_average_price.R vwap Execution algorithms A time-sliced order whose slice sizes follow the shape of the day’s volume. slices, over_minutes, volume_profile 200
ImplementationShortfallOrder R/orders_implementation_shortfall.R implementation_shortfall Execution algorithms A time-sliced order whose slices shrink, so most of it trades early. slices, over_minutes, urgency 200, or 202 when held
ParticipationOrder R/orders_participation.R participation Execution algorithms Trades a fixed share of the volume the market itself trades. participation_percent, most_slices 202
LiquiditySeekingOrder R/orders_liquidity_seeking.R liquidity_seeking Execution algorithms Shows nothing and strikes only when enough size appears at an acceptable price. limit_price, minimum_quantity 202
IcebergOrder R/orders_iceberg.R iceberg Execution algorithms Rests one slice at a time and places the next when that slice fills. slice_quantity, randomise_percent 200
AccumulationOrder R/orders_accumulation.R accumulation Execution algorithms Buys a fixed quantity at a fixed interval, like a SIP, each purchase resting on its own side of the book. every_minutes, purchases 200
ClosingPriceOrder R/orders_closing_price.R closing_price Execution algorithms Slices the order by volume through the half hour the day’s closing price is computed from. slices, window_start, volume_profile 202, or 200 inside the window
ScheduledOrder R/orders_scheduled.R scheduled Time-based Holds the order until a time of day and then places it. at_time 202
GoodTillTimeOrder R/orders_good_till_time.R good_till_time Time-based Places the order now and, at a time of day, cancels whatever has not filled or makes it marketable. until_time, at_expiry 200, or 202 when held
TimeStopOrder R/orders_time_stop.R time_stop Time-based Places an entry now and closes what filled at a time of day, or after some minutes. until_time or minutes 200, or 202 when held
SquareOffOrder R/orders_square_off.R square_off Time-based At a time of day, cancels resting orders and then closes the day’s positions on one product with limit orders. at_time, product, only_instruments 202
OpeningAuctionOrder R/orders_opening_auction.R opening_auction Time-based Places the order during the pre-open, so it fills at the opening auction’s price. at_time 202
BasketOrder R/orders_basket.R basket Multi-instrument Orders on several instruments placed in one request, each reported on its own. candidates, hedge_benefit 200
LeggedSpreadOrder R/orders_legged_spread.R legged_spread Multi-instrument A two-legged spread worked passively on the first leg and completed on the second at the price that makes the net. first_leg, second_leg, net_price 200
StrategyStopOrder R/orders_strategy_stop.R strategy_stop Multi-instrument A basket whose every leg is closed when the whole strategy’s profit or loss crosses a line. candidates, loss_limit, profit_target, hedge_benefit 200
ExposureHedgeOrder R/orders_exposure_hedge.R exposure_hedge Multi-instrument Trades one hedge instrument whenever the watched instruments’ net exposure leaves a band. watched, lower_band, upper_band, hedge_exposure_per_unit 202

Each class name links to its page in the reference, which lists every argument with its default. UBI’s glossary by family gives the rules UBI applies to each setting.

The table below counts the types in each family and splits them by their usual first answer; three types answer differently in some cases, as the last column of the table above shows. Every price trigger waits, and every linked order acts at once, which is a quick guide to whether an order is in the market as soon as you place it.

Family 200: acts at once 202: waits Types in all
Linked orders 8 0 8
Execution algorithms 5 3 8
Book-following limits 7 1 8
Price triggers 0 8 8
Stops and trailing 4 3 7
Plain and laddered 6 0 6
Time-based 2 3 5
Multi-instrument 3 1 4

How the classes fit together

Every class inherits from SyntheticOrder, which holds the ordinary order fields, called the template, and sends them with a synthetic object naming the type and holding its settings. A subclass adds only its own settings. The five multi-instrument classes also take small helper objects, one per instrument. The class diagram below shows the shape with a few of the fifty-four.

classDiagram
    class SyntheticOrder {
        instrument
        transaction_type
        product
        order_type
        quantity
        price
        reduce_only
        dry_run
        parent_id
        synthetic
        place()
        cancel()
        parent, orders, trades
    }
    class BracketOrder {
        stop_price
        stop_limit_price
        target_price
    }
    class HiddenStopOrder {
        trigger_level
        backstop_price
        backstop_limit_price
    }
    class BasketOrder {
        candidates
    }
    class ExposureHedgeOrder {
        watched
        lower_band
        upper_band
    }
    class OrderCandidate {
        instrument
        document()
    }
    class ExposureWatch {
        instrument
        exposure_per_unit
        document()
    }
    SyntheticOrder <|-- BracketOrder
    SyntheticOrder <|-- HiddenStopOrder
    SyntheticOrder <|-- BasketOrder
    SyntheticOrder <|-- ExposureHedgeOrder
    BasketOrder o-- "1..*" OrderCandidate
    ExposureHedgeOrder o-- "1..*" ExposureWatch

SyntheticOrder

The constructor of SyntheticOrder has the signature below.

SyntheticOrder$new(instrument, transaction_type, product, order_type, quantity, price = NULL, trigger_price = NULL, validity = NULL, disclosed_quantity = NULL, after_market = FALSE, tag = NULL, price_reference = NULL, quantity_reference = NULL, closes_position = FALSE, reduce_only = FALSE, hold_limits = NULL, dry_run = FALSE)

SyntheticOrder is the shared base of every class on this page, and it is the simple type itself. You normally construct one of its subclasses instead. In Python every argument after the instrument is keyword-only, so a class’s settings can never be passed in the wrong position. R has no keyword-only arguments, so the R classes take ordinary arguments in the same order, and every example names each argument after the instrument for the same reason: several of them are prices in rupees that are easy to swap.

The template fields are validated by UBI exactly as a plain order’s are, with the rules on Placing and reading orders, and most types use the template for every real order they send, changing only what they must. The package checks nothing before sending.

Parameters

The table below lists the template fields every class accepts. A class may make one of them required, fix it, or leave it out, and the reference shows the exact signature of each.

Name Type Required Default Description
instrument TradeableInstrument yes The instrument to trade.
transaction_type character yes buy or sell.
product character yes cnc, mis or nrml.
order_type character yes market, limit, sl or sl-m.
quantity integer or NULL yes The quantity in units, or NULL when a quantity_reference supplies it.
price numeric or NULL no NULL The template’s limit price in rupees.
trigger_price numeric or NULL no NULL The template’s own trigger price. In nine classes this argument means something else; see The trigger level.
validity character or NULL no NULL day or ioc.
disclosed_quantity integer or NULL no NULL The part of each order to show on the exchange.
after_market logical no FALSE TRUE sends after-market orders.
tag character or NULL no NULL A label of up to twenty letters and digits.
price_reference named list or NULL no NULL A price for UBI to work out, as on Price wrappers.
quantity_reference named list or NULL no NULL A quantity for UBI to work out, as on Positions.
closes_position logical no FALSE TRUE says every order this type sends closes a position, so it may use the part of a broker’s daily order cap that UBI keeps for exits.
reduce_only logical no FALSE TRUE has UBI check every leg against the net position just before sending it, and refuse any leg that would not reduce it. See Reduce-only orders.
hold_limits logical or NULL no NULL TRUE has UBI hold each order that would rest at the broker at a fixed limit price until the market reaches it, FALSE sends them as they come, and NULL leaves it to the type’s default. See Holding limit orders.
dry_run logical no FALSE TRUE has UBI build the first broker request and return it without recording or sending anything.

Every argument is stored as a public field of the same name, and the synthetic active binding gives the object that will be sent, as a named list: the type, every setting that is not NULL, closes_position and reduce_only when each is TRUE, and hold_limits when it is not NULL. Each class also has a public field SYNTHETIC_TYPE holding UBI’s name for its type, such as "bracket".

Not every type works a reference out. UBI resolves references for most single-instrument types, but nine types never call its resolver, so they need real numbers: ladder, two_sided_breakout, basket, oca, legged_spread, strategy_stop, exposure_hedge, square_off and daily_stop. UBI’s page on which order types resolve references has the full list.

place

The method place() sends a POST request to /api/orders/place, and it places orders.

This method sends the order to UBI’s order engine by calling the instrument’s place_order with the template fields and the synthetic object. It takes no arguments; everything, including dry_run, was given when the object was built.

Example

The example below builds the same bracket twice, first as a dry run to check it, then for real. A bracket buys ten shares at 1000 rupees and, on the first fill, arms a stop at 990 with a limit of 988 and a target at 1010. It is built from the class’s own documentation; no output was captured, because the real call places orders.

reliance <- Equity$new(exchange = "nse", symbol = "RELIANCE")

preview_order <- BracketOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "mis",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 10,
  price = 1000.0,
  stop_price = 990.0,
  stop_limit_price = 988.0,
  target_price = 1010.0,
  dry_run = TRUE
)
preview <- preview_order$place()
print(preview$request)

order <- BracketOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "mis",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 10,
  price = 1000.0,
  stop_price = 990.0,
  stop_limit_price = 988.0,
  target_price = 1010.0
)
print(order$synthetic)
answer <- order$place()
parent_id <- answer$parent_id

Worked out from the code, order$synthetic for these settings is a named list with four entries: type is "bracket", stop_price is 990, stop_limit_price is 988 and target_price is 1010. The client sends it to UBI as the JSON object {"type": "bracket", "stop_price": 990.0, "stop_limit_price": 988.0, "target_price": 1010.0}.

Returns

The method returns the named list that place_order returns. A type that acts at once answers with the broker’s answer plus a parent_id. A type that sends several orders at once, which is freeze_slicer, ladder, grid, two_sided_quote, basket, oco, bracket or two_sided_breakout, combines them into one answer with a legs list, one entry per order with its plan path, instrument_id, outcome, order_id and status_message, and one outcome: accepted when every order was, partial when only some were, which UBI answers with HTTP 207 and the package returns rather than signals, and otherwise unknown if any is unknown or rejected. A type that waits for a price or a time, or holds its limit orders, answers with HTTP 202, an outcome of armed, a broker and an order_id of NULL, and a parent_id. The answer below is UBI’s recorded example for a market_if_touched buy waiting for 995, from UBI’s offline test suite, as the JSON UBI sends; the package turns it into a named list, with each null read as NULL.

{
  "broker": null,
  "instrument_id": "11111111-1111-5111-8111-000000000001",
  "order_id": null,
  "outcome": "armed",
  "parent_id": "<uuid4>",
  "skipped": [],
  "status_message": "the order is recorded and will be placed when the price touches the level",
  "tag": null,
  "trigger_direction": "at_or_below",
  "trigger_level": "995"
}

The object keeps the parent_id itself, as described in After place, the parent.

Errors

The table below lists the conditions place() can signal. Each can be caught by its class name with tryCatch(..., ConflictError = function(error) ...).

Condition When
BadRequestError A template field is invalid, or one of the type’s own settings is missing or wrong.
LossLockoutError The day’s loss is past UBI’s daily loss limit.
ConflictError The engine refused to act on the account’s state, such as a post-only order that would cross the book or a reduce-only leg that would not reduce the position, or it had already started this order before a restart.
RateLimitError The broker’s daily order cap has no room for this order.
ServiceUnavailableError No broker could take the order, the order engine is not running, or a price UBI needed could not be read.
OrderOutcomeUnknownError The engine did not answer in time, so the order may still be placed. Read the order book before trying again.
UnifiedBrokerInterfaceError Any other failure reported by, or on the way to, UBI.

After place, the parent

UBI’s order engine records every synthetic order as a parent and answers with its parent_id, and the object keeps it. place() stores the parent_id from UBI’s answer on the object, and a dry run leaves it as NULL, because nothing was recorded. From then on the object can find and stop its own order through the instrument’s parent members, which Placing and reading orders documents. The table below lists what it offers.

Kind Member What it does Instrument member it calls
field parent_id UBI’s id for the order, or NULL before place() and after a dry run none
places orders cancel() Cancels the order with every leg it still has resting at a broker, so it places nothing more cancel_parent
active binding parent The order as the engine holds it now, with its state and its legs parent
active binding orders Today’s broker orders it placed, as a data frame, or NULL parent_orders
active binding trades Today’s trades in those orders, as a data frame, or NULL parent_trades

Each of the four signals ValueError while parent_id is NULL, because there is no parent to act on yet. cancel() does not close a position the order already opened; close it yourself, or use Account$flatten().

The example below arms a market-if-touched buy and cancels it again before it fires. No output was captured for it, because it records a real order.

order <- MarketIfTouchedOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "mis",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 10,
  price = 995.0,
  trigger_price = 995.0
)
order$place()
print(order$parent$state)
order$cancel()

Reduce-only orders

Any class can be made reduce-only with reduce_only = TRUE, which sends "reduce_only": true in the synthetic object. UBI then checks every leg against the net position in its instrument and product just before sending it, and lets the leg go only when it is on the side that closes the position and is no bigger than it. Anything else is refused with HTTP 409, which the package signals as ConflictError, and nothing is sent to a broker. The table below shows UBI’s rule.

Position held Leg Result
Long 75 Sell 50 Sent
Long 75 Sell 100 Refused, because it would leave a short of 25
Long 75 Buy 10 Refused, because it would add to the long
Short 40 Buy 40 Sent
Nothing Either side Refused

The check reads the position at the moment of sending, so a trigger that fires hours later is checked against the position as it is then. It does not count other orders still resting, so two reduce-only orders that are each smaller than the position can together be larger than it. A plain order is made reduce-only with SimpleOrder.

Holding limit orders

Since 2026-10-03 UBI runs every type other than simple and plan as a plan of that type’s preset, and many types now hold their limit orders in UBI’s virtual order book instead of resting them at the broker. A held order is sent only once the other side of the book reaches its price, so a limit the market never reaches costs no order message from the broker’s daily cap, at the price of its place in the queue. The hold_limits argument, which every class takes, decides: TRUE holds, FALSE sends the orders as they come, and NULL, the default, leaves it to the type.

The table below lists which types hold by default, while UBI’s UNIFIED_BROKER_INTERFACE_API_ORDER_HOLD_LIMITS switch is on, and what each still rests at the broker.

Type What is held What still rests at the broker
ScheduledOrder A limit order, from its time A market order
GoodTillTimeOrder A limit order, from placing; one still held at until_time is never sent Everything, when at_expiry is market
TimeStopOrder A limit entry, from placing The close
AccountConditionalOrder A limit order, from the moment the condition holds Everything, when action is cancel
LimitIfTouchedOrder, IndicatorTriggeredOrder, CrossInstrumentOrder The limit, from the touch, even if the price moves back Nothing
GoodTillTriggeredOrder The limit, from the touch, across days until valid_days runs out Nothing
BracketOrder, CoverOrder, ScaleOutOrder, OneTriggersOtherOrder A limit entry, from placing Every exit and the second order
OneCancelsAllOrder Every candidate Nothing
LadderOrder Each rung, at its own price Nothing
ScaleWithProfitTakerOrder Each rung, and again after its profit is taken Every profit-taker
TimeWeightedAveragePriceOrder, ImplementationShortfallOrder Each slice, from its turn, when the template is a limit order with a price that is neither ioc nor after-market Every slice of any other order, such as a market TWAP, which is sent unheld
FreezeSlicerOrder The whole order, whose slices then go out together Nothing

Every other type is not held unless it asks, and some refuse to be held because resting at the broker is what they are for: a GridOrder or TwoSidedQuoteOrder asking for it is refused with HTTP 400 and the rule not_holdable. A SimpleOrder refuses hold_limits = TRUE with HTTP 400. A PlanOrder follows UBI’s switch unless it says otherwise, and an OrderPart can give its own hold_limits to hold, for example, a profit target, which as a follow-on order would otherwise rest at the broker.

A held order is not in the broker’s order book until it is sent, so it is changed and cancelled through its parent: a held ladder rung is the plan part root.pieces.0, root.pieces.1 and so on, which PlanOrder$parts, modify_part() and cancel_part() reach without a broker message.

The trigger level

In nine classes the trigger_price argument is not the trigger of the order that is eventually sent. It is the level UBI watches before sending anything, and UBI calls that field trigger_price inside the synthetic object. To keep the two meanings apart, these classes store the argument as the field trigger_level, leave the template’s own trigger_price empty, and send the level as synthetic$trigger_price. The table below lists the nine and what each level watches.

Class What the level watches
MarketIfTouchedOrder The last traded price of this instrument
LimitIfTouchedOrder The last traded price of this instrument
CrossInstrumentOrder The last traded price of watch_instrument, a different instrument
IndicatorTriggeredOrder One field of the live quote, chosen by watch_field
GoodTillTriggeredOrder The last traded price, across days
CloseOnTriggerOrder The last traded price of this instrument
StopAndReverseOrder The last traded price of this instrument
HiddenStopOrder The bid when protecting a long position, the offer when protecting a short one
CandleCloseStopOrder The close of each bar, built from UBI’s own ticks

In all nine, trigger_price is a required argument and trigger_direction, at_or_above or at_or_below, is optional, because UBI works it out from the side. The example below shows the difference for a hidden stop.

order <- HiddenStopOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "mis",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 10,
  price = 990.0,
  trigger_price = 990.0,
  backstop_price = 980.0,
  backstop_limit_price = 978.0,
  dry_run = TRUE
)
print(order$trigger_price)
print(order$trigger_level)
print(order$synthetic)

Worked out from the code, order$trigger_price is NULL and order$trigger_level is 990. The synthetic named list holds type as "hidden_stop", trigger_price as 990, backstop_price as 980 and backstop_limit_price as 978, so the level travels to UBI inside the synthetic object and not as the template’s trigger.

Six of the nine also take trigger_on and hold_seconds, which choose the price compared with the level and how it must confirm, so that a single stray trade does not fire the order. They are MarketIfTouchedOrder, LimitIfTouchedOrder, CrossInstrumentOrder, GoodTillTriggeredOrder, CloseOnTriggerOrder and StopAndReverseOrder; the other three choose their own price, and UBI refuses trigger_on for them. The table below lists the values.

trigger_on Price compared with the level Fires on
last, UBI’s default The last traded price The first tick that reaches the level
bid The best bid The first tick that reaches the level
ask The best offer The first tick that reaches the level
mid Halfway between the best bid and offer The first tick that reaches the level
double_last The last traded price The second tick in a row that reaches the level
held The last traded price The first tick at least hold_seconds after the level was first reached, if every tick in between reached it too

AccountConditionalOrder is filed with the price triggers because it waits in the same way, but it watches the account rather than a price, so it takes no level of its own; its trigger_price argument is only the template’s ordinary trigger.

Orders on several instruments

Five classes act on more than one instrument, and they take helper objects rather than a single instrument. BasketOrder, OneCancelsAllOrder and StrategyStopOrder take a list of candidates, LeggedSpreadOrder takes a first_leg and a second_leg, and ExposureHedgeOrder takes a list of watched instruments plus the hedge instrument. In R these lists are ordinary list() values, which the package always sends to UBI as JSON arrays, even when they hold a single object.

UBI’s route still needs one instrument to anchor the request, so the first candidate’s instrument, or the first leg’s, becomes the order’s instrument. A dry run of a basket prepares only that first candidate’s order. BasketOrder, OneCancelsAllOrder and StrategyStopOrder signal ValueError when given no candidate at all, because there would be nothing to anchor the request.

A candidate inherits the whole template.

UBI lays each candidate’s fields over the whole template, so a template price is carried into a candidate that sets order_type to market, and UBI then refuses the market order because it carries a price. Give such a template no price, or give each candidate its own. The same trap applies to OneTriggersOtherOrder’s then_order_type.

OrderCandidate

The constructor of OrderCandidate has the signature below.

OrderCandidate$new(instrument, transaction_type = NULL, product = NULL, order_type = NULL, validity = NULL, quantity = NULL, price = NULL, trigger_price = NULL, tag = NULL)

An OrderCandidate is one leg of a multi-instrument order: an instrument, and any of eight template fields it overrides. A field left as NULL takes the template’s value. Its document() method gives the object UBI reads, as a named list with instrument_id and every field that is set.

Parameters

The table below lists its arguments.

Name Type Required Default Description
instrument TradeableInstrument yes The instrument this leg trades.
transaction_type, product, order_type, validity, quantity, price, trigger_price, tag as on SyntheticOrder no NULL The template fields this leg overrides.

ExposureWatch

The constructor of ExposureWatch has the signature below.

ExposureWatch$new(instrument, exposure_per_unit = NULL)

An ExposureWatch names one instrument whose net position counts towards the exposure an ExposureHedgeOrder keeps inside its band, and how much exposure each unit carries. UBI has no option pricing model, so the delta of an option is yours to supply as exposure_per_unit. Its document() method gives the object UBI reads.

Parameters

The table below lists its arguments.

Name Type Required Default Description
instrument Instrument yes The instrument whose net position is counted.
exposure_per_unit numeric or NULL no NULL The exposure one unit carries, such as an option’s delta. UBI counts 1 when it is NULL.

By family

The sections below group the fifty-four classes into UBI’s eight families, which UBI’s documentation uses to make the list easier to scan; neither UBI’s code nor this package groups them. Each section has one example, taken from the classes’ own documentation, and every example is a dry run. In the examples, reliance and infosys are Equity objects, nifty_call and nifty_put are EquityIndexOption objects, and nifty_future is an EquityIndexFutures object.

Plain and laddered

These six types act at once and place everything they need when you ask. SimpleOrder is a plain order, useful by name only to set closes_position. FreezeSlicerOrder splits an order above the exchange’s freeze quantity into slices of whole lots at one broker, so 55 NIFTY lots of 65 under a limit of 3,511 go as 28 and 27 lots, and by default holds the whole order until the market reaches its price. LadderOrder shares the quantity across evenly spaced limit orders, and by default holds each rung until the market reaches that rung’s price; with hold_limits = FALSE every rung rests at the broker at once. GridOrder rests buys below and sells above the market and replaces each fill with its opposite, and most_inventory caps the position a trending market can build. ScaleWithProfitTakerOrder is a ladder whose every filled rung gets a profit-taker profit_points better, and is placed again once that profit is taken, up to most_cycles times. TwoSidedQuoteOrder keeps a bid and an offer half_spread_points either side of the fair price, leaning both away from the inventory it builds by skew_ticks per order’s worth held; every move of the fair price by a step costs two modifications, so keep step_ticks wide. Neither of the last two finishes on its own, so stop them with cancel().

The example below spreads a buy of 100 shares over three limit orders between 995 and 1000 rupees, which share it as 34, 33 and 33.

order <- LadderOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "cnc",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 100,
  price = 1000.0,
  from_price = 995.0,
  to_price = 1000.0,
  steps = 3,
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

Linked orders

These eight types place orders that watch each other, so a fill on one changes, places or cancels another. A linked exit is reduced by what its sibling filled rather than cancelled, so a position is never left unprotected. Every stop is a stop-limit, so a stop always needs both stop_price and stop_limit_price. The list below describes each of the eight.

  • BracketOrder arms a stop and a target on the entry’s first fill, even a partial one, and grows them as more fills.
  • CoverOrder is a bracket with a compulsory stop and no target.
  • OneCancelsOtherOrder protects a position you already hold. Set transaction_type to the side that opened it, so a long position is protected by asking for buy.
  • ScaleOutOrder takes a position off in tranches at several target_prices and moves the stop to breakeven after breakeven_after of them fill. The target_prices may be given as c(...) or as list(...), and are always sent as a JSON array.
  • OneTriggersOtherOrder places a second order, described by the then_ settings, sized to what the first filled.
  • TwoSidedBreakoutOrder rests native buy and sell stops around a range, so they fire at exchange speed even if UBI is down, and cancels the one that did not fire. Its stop and target are distances from the entry’s fill, so they suit a break either way.
  • OneCancelsAllOrder takes several candidates on different instruments and cancels the rest on the first fill.
  • AttachedHedgeOrder hedges each fill of the entry in hedge_instrument, sized by a fixed ratio or, for an option entry, by its Black-76 delta at delta_volatility, and rounded to whole lots of the hedge.

The example below buys ten shares at 1000 rupees with a stop at 990 and a target at 1010.

order <- BracketOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "mis",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 10,
  price = 1000.0,
  stop_price = 990.0,
  stop_limit_price = 988.0,
  target_price = 1010.0,
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

Price triggers

These eight types send nothing until a level is reached, so their first answer is 202 with an outcome of armed, and the seven that watch a price store their level as trigger_level, as The trigger level explains. MarketIfTouchedOrder buys on a dip or sells on a rise, which a native stop cannot do, because a native stop only fires when the price moves against you. LimitIfTouchedOrder rests a limit at limit_price once touched. CrossInstrumentOrder watches a different instrument, so an option can be exited when the index crosses a level rather than when its own thin book spikes. IndicatorTriggeredOrder watches one field of the quote, most usefully average_price. GoodTillTriggeredOrder is what brokers sell as GTT: it waits across days, 30 by default and up to 365. CloseOnTriggerOrder is a stop that first cancels every order resting on the instrument, at every broker, to free the margin they hold, and then closes the whole position held when it fires. StopAndReverseOrder does the same and then opens the same size the other way, either after the close has filled (method = "sequential") or as one order for twice the position (method = "double"). AccountConditionalOrder waits on the account instead: when available_balance, day_pnl or open_positions reaches account_level, it sends the order, or, with action = "cancel", it cancels an order it sent at once.

The example below sells ten shares held for delivery if the price falls to 950, resting a limit at 951.

order <- GoodTillTriggeredOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "sell",
  product = "cnc",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 10,
  price = 951.0,
  trigger_price = 950.0,
  limit_price = 951.0,
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

Stops and trailing

These seven types protect a position. Two of them keep the stop inside UBI, where the book cannot see it: HiddenStopOrder watches the bid or the offer, and CandleCloseStopOrder fires only when a whole bar closes past the level, so a brief wick does not stop you out. A hidden stop protects nothing while UBI is down, which is what the optional backstop is for, a real stop-loss limit placed at the broker at once. The other four put a real stop at the broker: TrailingStopOrder moves its trigger up with the market and never down, TrailingEntryOrder is its mirror for entering, AverageTrueRangeTrailOrder trails by a multiple of the recent average true range, and DailyStopOrder re-places a native stop every trading morning, because native stops expire at the end of the day. SteppedStopOrder moves a native stop to set levels as the profit from entry_price passes each rule’s gain, and can switch to trailing at the last rule. With activate_at, a TrailingStopOrder places nothing until the price reaches that level, which makes it a trailing take-profit. A hidden stop with a backstop answers HTTP 200 with a legs list holding the backstop at the path root.children.1.

The example below buys ten shares and trails a stop five rupees behind the best price, with its limit two rupees past the trigger.

order <- TrailingStopOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "mis",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 10,
  price = 1000.0,
  trail_points = 5.0,
  stop_limit_offset = 2.0,
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

Book-following limits

These eight types manage a limit order against the market. PegOrder re-prices it to your own side’s best price, the midpoint or the other side, and every re-price is a real modification that loses the order’s place in the queue. ChaserOrder starts on its own side and steps towards the other until it fills, crossing outright after cross_after_seconds and never beyond cap_price. PostOnlyOrder checks the book before sending, because Indian exchanges have no post-only flag; with on_crossing = "refuse" an order that would cross is refused with HTTP 409. DiscretionaryOrder shows one price and takes a slightly worse one when it comes within discretion_points. VirtualLimitOrder holds the limit inside UBI until the other side reaches it, and with paper = TRUE never sends anything at all; every plain day limit order now runs as this type. MarketableLimitOrder is a market order with a worst price: a limit buffer_ticks past the other side’s best price, two by default, moved after that price until it fills and cancelled after fill_within_seconds, thirty by default, and refused with HTTP 409 when nobody is on the other side or the quote is missing or stale; every plain market order that is not after-market now runs as this type with the defaults. UnderlyingPegOrder moves a resting limit by delta times the move of watch_instrument, such as an option bid following the index, without reading the option’s own thin book. VolatilityOrder states an option order as an implied volatility and lets UBI work the premium out with Black-76, re-pricing as the underlying and time move; its price is the worst it will accept.

The example below keeps a buy of ten shares pegged to the midpoint, never paying more than 1005 rupees.

order <- PegOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "mis",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 10,
  price = 1000.0,
  reference = "mid",
  cap_price = 1005.0,
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

Execution algorithms

These eight types work a large order into the market over time or against liquidity. TimeWeightedAveragePriceOrder sends equal slices at even intervals, VolumeWeightedAveragePriceOrder sizes them to the day’s usual volume, and ImplementationShortfallOrder makes them shrink so that most of the order trades early, becoming a plain time-weighted order at an urgency of 0. ParticipationOrder trades a fixed share of the market’s own volume. LiquiditySeekingOrder shows nothing and strikes only when minimum_quantity is visible at limit_price or better. IcebergOrder shows one slice at a time. AccumulationOrder buys a fixed quantity at a fixed interval, like a SIP, never paying more than a limit order’s price. ClosingPriceOrder is a volume-weighted order spread over the half hour from 15:00 to 15:30, from which NSE and BSE compute an equity’s closing price, which is the nearest to a market-on-close order there is for futures, options and intraday orders. The three time-sliced types and AccumulationOrder work a price_reference out afresh for every order they send, while the others work it out once, when UBI takes the order.

The example below buys 600 shares in six slices over thirty minutes, each priced to fill at once.

order <- TimeWeightedAveragePriceOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "cnc",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 600,
  price_reference = list(kind = "marketable"),
  slices = 6,
  over_minutes = 30.0,
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

Time-based

These five types act at a time of day, written as HH:MM or HH:MM:SS in India time, on the instrument’s own exchange trading calendar. On a trading day a time that has already passed is refused rather than taken to mean tomorrow, and on a weekend or an exchange holiday it means that time on the next trading day. ScheduledOrder holds the order until at_time. GoodTillTimeOrder places it now and cancels what has not filled at until_time, filling the gap between the exchanges’ day and ioc validities; with at_expiry = "market" it makes what is left marketable instead. OpeningAuctionOrder places the order during the pre-open, so it fills at the opening auction’s price; only NSE and BSE equities and exchange-traded funds and NSE futures have a pre-open, and UBI refuses the rest. TimeStopOrder closes what the entry filled at until_time or after minutes, cancelling the unfilled part first. SquareOffOrder closes the day’s positions on one product at at_time with limit orders, after cancelling their resting orders, instead of leaving it to the broker’s automatic square-off with its market order and fee. It leaves overnight positions alone, which is the difference from Account$flatten(), and it sets closes_position by default.

The example below closes every intraday position at 15:05.

order <- SquareOffOrder$new(
  reliance,
  at_time = "15:05",
  product = "mis",
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

SquareOffOrder takes no side, order type or quantity, because UBI decides them for every closing order from the positions. The route still needs a template, so the package fills it with placeholders, a sell market order for a quantity of 1. It also translates product into the positions’ spelling, so the example sends {"type": "square_off", "at_time": "15:05", "product": "intraday", "closes_position": true}. The instrument you pass only anchors the request and does not limit what is closed; only_instruments does that.

Multi-instrument

These four types trade several instruments together, as Orders on several instruments explains. BasketOrder places one order per candidate and does nothing afterwards. LeggedSpreadOrder rests the first leg and, as it fills, takes the second at whatever price makes the pair come to net_price; between the two fills the position is one-legged, because only an exchange’s own multi-leg order can guarantee a net price. StrategyStopOrder places a basket and closes every leg when the combined profit or loss falls to loss_limit or rises to profit_target. ExposureHedgeOrder adds up the watched instruments’ net positions, each weighted by its exposure per unit, and trades the hedge instrument whenever the total leaves the band; UBI decides the side and quantity of every hedge, so the package sends a placeholder buy market template for a quantity of 1.

The example below keeps the net delta of two NIFTY options between -75 and 75 by trading a NIFTY future.

order <- ExposureHedgeOrder$new(
  nifty_future,
  watched = list(
    ExposureWatch$new(nifty_call, exposure_per_unit = 0.5),
    ExposureWatch$new(nifty_put, exposure_per_unit = -0.4)
  ),
  lower_band = -75.0,
  upper_band = 75.0,
  product = "nrml",
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

Plans: combining the types

A plan is UBI’s fifty-fourth type, and it describes an order as a tree of parts rather than naming one fixed type. That lets several of the types above be combined in one order, such as a bracket whose entry waits for the price to touch a level, or an entry whose fills are protected by a stop and a trailing stop at once. PlanOrder, in R/orders_plan.R, takes the same order template as every other class plus a plan argument, and the parts of the tree come from the R/orders_plan_parts_*.R files, one class per part.

The table below lists the parts by kind.

Kind Classes What they decide
Node OrderPart One order, and every setting below that shapes it. It can also give its own instrument, quantity, transaction_type, product, validity and tag, which is how one plan trades several instruments.
Joins ThenPart, EitherPart, TogetherPart, SequencePart, RepeatPart, UsingPart The shape of the tree: an order that starts another when it fills; several at once where a fill on one acts on the others; several sent together, or one after another; one order sent again on a schedule; and one order split into pieces, each run as a plan of its own.
Presets Preset An existing type used as an ingredient, such as Preset$new("bracket", stop_price = 990.0, stop_limit_price = 988.0, target_price = 1010.0).
Triggers PriceCrosses, Trails, CandleCloses, AccountCondition, LimitMarketable, TimeAt, TimeAfter, TimeBefore, TimeFrom, AllConditions, AnyCondition When an order is sent.
Pricing FixedPricing, MarketablePricing, NativeStopPricing, TrailPricing, PegPricing, ChasePricing, FollowInstrumentPricing, OptionModelPricing, StagesPricing with StageRule, FromFillPricing, FromParentFillPricing The price it is sent at, and whether that price follows the market, another instrument or an earlier fill.
Pricing modifiers CapModifier, DiscretionModifier A worst price the rule may not pass, and a little room to trade past the price. They go beside the pricing rule.
Executions AllAtOnceExecution, IcebergExecution, TwapExecution, VwapExecution, FrontLoadedExecution, ParticipationExecution, BookDepthExecution, TopUpExecution, DailyExecution, LadderExecution, FreezeLimitExecution How the order is sent: whole, or in pieces over time, by volume or by price. One execution can work each piece of another, such as TWAP slices each shown as an iceberg.
Guard PostOnlyGuard Keeps an order from trading at once, so it only ever rests in the book.
Lifetime Lifetime When an order ends by itself, at a time, after a while or when a condition holds, and what it does then.
Venues PreOpenVenue, PaperVenue Sends the order in the pre-open session, or fills it on paper only.
Quantities PositionQuantity, ParentFillQuantity, ParentFillDeltaQuantity Sizes the order from a position, from what an earlier order filled, or from the delta of an option the plan traded.

Every part has a document() method that returns the named list UBI reads. One R detail differs from Python here: repeat is a reserved word in R, so RepeatPart$document() names its key with backticks, `repeat`, and the client still sends it to UBI as the JSON key "repeat".

An OrderPart can also take side = "protect", which trades against the position the template’s side opened, so a buy’s protecting order is a sell. Presets are merged first and the order’s own values after them: triggers from several sources must all hold, and a later pricing rule replaces an earlier one.

The example below is a limit buy whose every fill is protected by a stop resting at the broker and by a stop that trails five rupees behind the market. The two stops share one quantity, so as one fills the other shrinks.

order <- PlanOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "mis",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 10,
  price = 1000.0,
  plan = ThenPart$new(
    first = OrderPart$new(),
    each_fill = EitherPart$new(
      children = list(
        OrderPart$new(
          side = "protect",
          pricing = NativeStopPricing$new(
            trigger_price = 980.0,
            limit_price = 978.0
          )
        ),
        OrderPart$new(
          side = "protect",
          pricing = TrailPricing$new(
            points = 5.0,
            limit_offset = 1.0
          )
        )
      ),
      sibling_rule = "reduce"
    )
  ),
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

UBI checks the whole plan before recording or sending anything, and a plan with any problem is refused with HTTP 400 listing every problem with the path of the part it is in, such as root.each_fill.children.1. A dry run answers with the plan as it would run, every default written out, under plan. A plan that sends nothing at once answers HTTP 202 with an outcome of armed.

The example below buys in six slices over an hour, each slice shown to the market ten shares at a time, pegged to the bid but never above 1010, and ends whatever is left at 14:30.

order <- PlanOrder$new(
  reliance,
  transaction_type = "buy",
  product = "mis",
  order_type = "limit",
  quantity = 120,
  price = 1000.0,
  plan = OrderPart$new(
    pricing = PegPricing$new(reference = "own_touch"),
    cap = CapModifier$new(worst_price = 1010.0),
    execution = TwapExecution$new(slices = 6, over_minutes = 60),
    inner_execution = IcebergExecution$new(visible_quantity = 10),
    lifetime = Lifetime$new(at_time = "14:30")
  ),
  dry_run = TRUE
)
answer <- order$place()

Because Preset takes any name and any settings through its ... argument, every preset UBI offers works here as soon as UBI adds it.

Acting on one part

Once a plan is placed, each of its parts is named by a path, such as root.first for a bracket’s entry and root.each_fill.children.0 and root.each_fill.children.1 for its stop and target. The table below lists the three members that work with those paths.

Member What it does
parts An active binding giving a data frame of the plan’s parts, one row per path, with each part’s state: pending, waiting, working or done.
cancel_part(part, dry_run = FALSE) Cancels one part while the rest of the plan carries on. A part whose turn has not come is never sent, and a part that has sent orders sends no more and has its resting orders cancelled.
modify_part(part, price = NULL, trigger_price = NULL, quantity = NULL, dry_run = FALSE) Changes a part that has not sent anything yet, such as a bracket’s stop before the entry fills. Nothing is sent to a broker until the part’s turn comes.

They call TradeableInstrument$cancel_parent() and TradeableInstrument$modify_order() with the plan’s parent_id and the part’s path, which can also be used directly.

The Atlas rows that need no class

UBI’s order engine was designed from a catalogue called the Synthetic Order Atlas. Most of its rows are classes here, but some need no class, because each is already reachable another way, as the table below shows. SimpleOrder and VirtualLimitOrder are the reverse: they are in UBI’s registry without being Atlas rows.

Atlas row How to get it
Marketable limit buy_at_marketable_price and sell_at_marketable_price, or a list(kind = "marketable") price reference
Market-to-limit The same marketable price reference
Immediate-or-cancel validity = "ioc" on any order
Stop-market A plain place_order() with order_type = "sl-m" and a trigger_price
Stop entry A plain place_order() with order_type = "sl" or "sl-m" on the entry side
One-updates-other How every linked type already behaves: a fill on one leg reduces its sibling
Kill switch Account$flatten()
Daily loss lockout A UBI setting; an order past the limit signals LossLockoutError
Snap order (G3) A limit priced from the book when it is sent: a price_reference such as list(kind = "marketable") or list(kind = "bid_level", offset_ticks = 1)
Midprice order (G4) list(kind = "mid") for a price worked out once, or PegOrder with reference = "mid" for one that stays at the midpoint

The Atlas also has a group G, seventeen further types found in a second sweep of broker catalogues. UBI built the rest of them on 2026-09-27. Eleven became new types, each with its class here, from OpeningAuctionOrder (G1) to AccountConditionalOrder (G17). Four became settings on existing types, as the table below shows, and G3 and G4 are the two rows above.

Atlas row Setting On
G5, a limit that becomes marketable at a time at_expiry = "market" GoodTillTimeOrder
G9, a trailing take-profit activate_at TrailingStopOrder
G10, triggers that confirm trigger_on and hold_seconds The six price triggers listed under The trigger level
G11, reduce-only reduce_only Every class

What the package does not check

Nothing on this page is validated before sending. The classes do not check that a stop is below an entry, that a time is in the future, that a candidate list has no repeats or that two instruments are related; UBI does all of that and answers with a BadRequestError naming the problem. The Python library’s own offline check on 2026-09-26 compared every class’s synthetic object with UBI’s documented example for its type and found all forty-two classes of that day matched; the eleven classes added on 2026-09-27 were built from UBI’s glossary and have not been through that comparison. On 2026-10-07 every type, including the base class, was built in both Python and R against fake clients, from the required arguments only, from every argument, and with one-element lists where the type takes a list, and the JSON body each side sent to /api/orders/place matched in all 119 cases, so the R classes send exactly what the Python classes send. Whether UBI accepts each class’s settings, rather than only their shape, has not yet been confirmed with a dry run against a running engine.
